title: Permafrost Is Thawing From the Inside Out in Canada's North
summary:
Deep in Canada's Northwest Territories, the ground itself is changing. Permafrost, ground that stays frozen for at least two years in a row, is thawing in surprising ways. In some places, it is melting from the inside out and setting off a new kind of landslide.

The Mackenzie River winds through this frozen landscape. It is North America's largest northward-flowing river and drains about 20 percent of Canada's land. For thousands of years, permafrost held the region steady. But as the climate warms, that stability is crumbling.

In 2017 and 2018, two huge landslides struck the central Mackenzie Valley, moving 4.5 and 18 million cubic meters of frozen ground. What puzzled scientists was what the landslides carried: large chunks of earth that were still frozen, which had slid hundreds of meters. Normally, permafrost melts from the top down into a slow muddy slide, but these slides were different. Ground observations showed the sliding happened about 20 meters below the surface.

In 2019, permafrost geologist Joseph Young, then a PhD student at the University of Alberta, flew to a remote field site and saw slopes collapsing with landslides everywhere. He and a team from the university tracked ground temperatures from 2020 to 2022. They concluded that wildfires from decades earlier and rising summer temperatures had formed cracks in the ground. Water seeped in through the cracks and warmed the permafrost from below, weakening its base. The researchers named the new phenomenon permafrost detachment slides and reported it in the journal Geophysical Research Letters.

Warming and wildfire together push heat underground over decades, weakening the permafrost base. Thawing also releases trapped metals into rivers, turning some orange, and studies estimate it could cause more than $50 billion in damage to buildings and roads in Alaska by 2050.
why_it_matters: Warming and wildfire together push heat underground over decades, weakening the permafrost that holds northern land steady. As it thaws, it can damage buildings and roads and release trapped metals into rivers, so understanding this new kind of landslide matters for the people and places that depend on frozen ground.

background_read: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen for at least two years in a row, and it acts like a solid base that holds northern landscapes steady.
For thousands of years, permafrost has held the region around the Mackenzie River steady, keeping slopes and soil in place.
When the climate warms, the frozen ground can thaw, and water seeping through cracks warmed the permafrost from below and weakened its base.
That weakening can set off landslides that move large chunks of still-frozen earth, and thawing can also release trapped metals into rivers and damage buildings and roads.
